events.summary: Heart rhythm: The heart is beating at a normal speed in a regular rhythm, but the machine's tracing shows some differences in the way the electrical signal spreads through the heart.

limitations: The machine-generated report has NOT been reviewed or confirmed by a cardiologist; machine ECG reports are known to be over-cautious and can flag findings that turn out to be normal for a given person.
Only 4 of the 12 ECG leads are shown in the image, so a full picture of the heart's electrical activity is not available here.
No clinical information (age, symptoms, medications, or medical history) was provided, which is essential for putting any of these findings in context.
This tool is a research prototype and cannot provide medical advice or diagnosis.
uncertainty: A QRS axis of 129 degrees and a QRS duration of 134 ms are outside typical ranges, but what these mean for this specific person's health can only be judged by a doctor who knows their full medical history.
Nonspecific ST-T changes can appear in many situations, including normal variations, and do not by themselves point to one particular cause.
The irregularity score of 0.036 suggests the rhythm is very regular, but a small amount of beat-to-beat variation is normal and expected.

findings.statement: The heart rate is 74 beats per minute, which is a normal resting speed, and the beats appear very regular with almost no variation between them.

The machine detected something called a 'right bundle branch block', which means the electrical signal may be taking a slightly unusual path through the lower part of the heart — this shows up as a wider-than-usual heartbeat signal (the QRS part) on the tracing.
findings.evidence: qrs_ms: 134.0 (wider than the typical upper limit of about 120 ms); machine report: 'Right bundle branch block'

findings.statement: The machine also flagged 'right axis deviation' and 'nonspecific ST-T changes', meaning the direction of the electrical signal and the shape of part of the wave look a little different from the most common pattern — but the machine itself called these changes 'nonspecific', meaning they can have many innocent causes.
findings.evidence: qrs_axis_degrees: 129; machine report: 'Right axis deviation | Inferior/lateral ST-T changes are nonspecific'

payload.title: What the findings may mean
payload.text: The chest X-ray may show an enlarged heart shadow and patchy, hazy areas in the right lung and left lower lung, which could suggest fluid, infection, or other changes in the lung tissue. The ECG shows a normal heart rate of 74 beats per minute in a very regular rhythm, but the electrical signal through the lower part of the heart still appears to travel an unusual path — a pattern called right bundle branch block — and the direction and shape of the signal look a little different from the most common pattern. Compared with the two earlier visits (day 0 and day 2), the heart rate has come down from 85 and then 81 beats per minute to 74 now, which could be worth mentioning to the care team. Importantly, the earlier visits flagged something called an 'inferior infarct' and, on day 0, wording about possible 'myocardial injury/ischemia' and 'edema' — those specific labels do not appear in today's reports, though this does not necessarily mean those concerns are gone, as automated tools can vary from reading to reading.

payload.text: It may be worth asking the care team whether there are any gentle movement or light activity routines that would be suitable right now. These are only topics to raise — the care team should guide any actual changes.

payload.title: Questions to ask your doctor
payload.text: This summary was made by a research prototype using automated tools — it is not medical advice and has not been reviewed by a doctor or radiologist. Please bring this printout to the care team and ask them to explain what these findings mean for this specific person. Some questions that may help start that conversation: 'Have the lung changes improved, stayed the same, or got worse compared with before?' 'What does the right bundle branch block mean for her, given her history?' 'The earlier reports mentioned an inferior infarct and possible injury — is that still a concern?' Always follow the guidance of the qualified medical team caring for her.

limitations: This virtual patient combines an ECG and a chest X-ray from two different real people. The ECG report was written by a machine and not confirmed by a cardiologist.
